title: How thick a year is here
task: Turn this year's snow into the ice it will become.
scene: Brandt has the pit wall photographed. Last summer's surface is marked thirty-two centimetres down. The snow above it weighs about a third of what solid ice would.
assumes: snow turns into ice by being squashed under the snow that falls on top of it
density is how much a given amount of something weighs
takeaway: A year's snowfall means nothing until it is written as the ice it will become.
question: How much ice will this year's snow turn into?
why: Snow and ice are the same stuff at different weights, so a thickness of snow is not a thickness of record. Scale it by how heavy the snow is against solid ice, and you get what it will become once the air is squeezed out. That is the only form in which two places can be compared. Here a year is about twelve centimetres of ice. A site by the coast gets a metre.
answerText: About 0.12 metres of ice — a third of the snow, because the snow is a third as heavy.

estimate.prompt: Last summer's surface sits thirty-two centimetres down, in snow about a third as heavy as solid ice.
estimate.question: How much ice will this year's snow turn into?
estimate.relationship: Ice = the snow thickness × how heavy the snow is ÷ how heavy solid ice is.
estimate.explanation: The water tile does not belong. This is snow turning into ice, and liquid water is never part of the record.

title: Why the hole is on the dome
task: Say what drilling on the high point buys.
scene: Pär Lindqvist, the drill engineer, has the hole down at two thousand metres. On the wall is a map with three abandoned sites, all of them on slopes. Vestri Dome is the high point here.
assumes: ice spreads outwards from the high points of an ice sheet
takeaway: A core is a column of what fell above it only where the ice has not travelled sideways.
question: What does drilling on the dome buy that a site on a slope cannot?
why: An ice sheet spreads outwards from its high points, like very slow treacle. On a slope, the ice at a given depth came from somewhere uphill. So a core there mixes one place's weather with a long journey, and nothing afterwards can separate them. Under a dome the ice goes almost straight down, so the column under the drill is very nearly the snow that fell on it. Domes charge for that. High, cold, dry, thin layers.
answerText: The ice at each depth fell close to where it sits now, so the core is one place's weather stacked up.

choices: The ice at each depth fell near this spot, and did not arrive from somewhere else.
The ice is colder at the top, which slows down the changes inside it.
Snow falls hardest at the high point, which makes the yearly layers thick.
The rock under a dome is flattest, which keeps a long hole straight.
rebuttals: Ice at the summit is colder, and cold is not what makes depth match time.
Domes are the driest part of an ice sheet, not the snowiest. Thin layers are the price of drilling here.
The shape of the rock matters to the deepest ice, and it is not why the site sits on the high point.

title: What makes one year different from the next
task: Match each thing in the ice to what put it there.
scene: A metre of core from sixty metres down is on the light table. Ines Okonkwo, the chronology lead, has four things marked on it and wants each one explained before it is cut.
assumes: snow that falls in summer sits in different conditions from snow that falls in winter
takeaway: A year is counted from several signals that agree, not from one that looks convincing.
why: No single marker survives all the way down a core. So a year is counted where several different signals line up. Coarse crystals grow on a summer surface left out in the open. A spike in electricity is acid, and volcanic acid arrives in one season. Dust blows in from far away and peaks with the winds there. The banding is bubbles changing as each layer was squashed. Three of four agreeing is a year.

scenarios: A band of large, loosely joined crystals
A narrow spike in how well the ice carries electricity
A rise in fine mineral dust
Light and dark bands about a centimetre apart
choices: A summer surface that sat out in the open and grew coarse before it was buried.
Acid from a volcano, laid down over a season or two and then gone.
Windier months on faraway continents, carried here and settled out.
Bubbles changing size through the year as the snow was squashed.
rebuttals: Electricity responds to acid. The band of coarse crystals is a surface that was left out in the open.
Dust is delivered from far away, and it does not follow the crystals growing on this surface.
The banding follows how the snow was squashed, rather than what blew in from somewhere else.

title: The run through the brittle zone
task: Put the steps in the order that brings a cracking section up whole.
scene: The barrel is at seven hundred and eighty metres, in the depth band where the ice comes up cracked. The winch, the fluid and the storage are all set for ordinary ice.
assumes: air trapped deep in the ice is squeezed to the pressure of the ice around it
takeaway: Ice brought up badly is a shorter record, not a cheaper one.
why: Deep down, the bubbles are squeezed far harder than the air at the surface. Bring that ice up quickly and it cracks itself apart. Each step here buys the next one. A slow lift is less of a shock. Resting at hole temperature lets the pressure even out. Writing down the breaks fixes which depth each piece came from, while somebody still knows. Cutting first destroys that, and cuts ice that is still moving.

cards: Slow the winch through the band where the bubbles are squeezed hardest.
Let the section sit in the trench at hole temperature before anybody handles it.
Write down every break and where it is, before anything moves off the barrel.
Carry the section to the storage trench and leave it to settle.
Cut it up and share it out once it has stopped cracking.

title: The metre with no label
task: Decide what an unlabelled section is good for.
scene: A section has come to the line with its depth mark broken. Holt can place it to within about four metres from the run sheet. The isotope team has asked for it.
assumes: a measurement belongs to the depth it came from, and to no other
takeaway: A sample with no depth is a measurement of nothing in particular.
question: What should the section be used for?
why: A depth is what turns a measurement into a statement about a year. Four metres here is thirty-odd years, so an isotope value off this section cannot be put anywhere in the record. The ice is still perfectly good for anything a depth does not enter. How heavy it is. What the crystals look like. How the drill is performing. What matters is that the doubt travels with the sample. The danger is somebody later who never hears about it.
answerText: Work that does not need a precise depth. How heavy it is, what the crystals look like, how the drill is doing. The four metres of doubt gets written against it.

choices: Work that can live with four metres of doubt, with the doubt written down.
Isotope work, since four metres is small next to the whole core.
Nothing. An unplaced section is thrown out so it cannot spoil the record.
Anything, once the run sheet is used to give it its most likely depth.
rebuttals: Four metres is about thirty years here, which is bigger than most of what the isotopes are used to find.
Throwing it out wastes measurements that never needed a depth in the first place.
A most likely depth writes a guess into the record, in the same handwriting as the measurements.

title: Clean until it was handled
task: Work out where the salt came from.
scene: Elena Cruz has a salt result four times higher than the run before it. The blank, the run order and the section's handling record are on the bench.
assumes: a blank goes through the whole process with no sample in it, so it measures the process
takeaway: A blank measures the process, so anything it shows was never evidence about the ice.
why: The blank before the sample is normal, and the blank after it is high. That puts the salt inside the run rather than inside the ice. The trim was done properly, so the outside of the section is out. The second core holds the same year with no salt in it, so that year's weather is out too. What names the source is not the loud number. It is which quiet ones stayed quiet.
answerText: Something in the laboratory got into the run. The blank afterwards is high, and the second core holds the same year clean.

choices: Sea salt reached the plateau in the year this ice fell.
Something in the laboratory got into the run and stayed there.
The outside of the section was not trimmed off.
The second core missed the layer, so it is the wrong thing to compare with.
choiceMechanisms: A storm carried sea air a long way inland, and the ice recorded it.
The process itself added salt, and went on adding it to what came after.
Drill fluid and handling left salt on the outside of the section.
The second hole missed the layer completely.
text.headline: One salt result is four times the run before it — and the blank that followed it is high too.

title: The depth the counting runs out
task: Find the depth where the layers stop being countable.
scene: The layer-thickness log runs from the surface to the bottom of the core. The line can tell apart two bands three millimetres apart and no closer. Okonkwo needs to know where the ice crosses that.
assumes: layers are stretched thinner as the ice underneath them spreads outwards
takeaway: A count ends where the instrument stops telling one year from the next.
question: The line separates bands three millimetres apart and no closer. At what depth does a year get that thin?
why: Ice spreads outwards under its own weight, so every layer is stretched thinner as it sinks. The deeper it goes, the faster that happens. At the surface a year here is about twelve centimetres. Two kilometres down the same year is a few millimetres. Where the layers close to within what the line can separate, the counting stops. Not because the years have gone, but because two of them cannot be told apart.
answerText: About 2,180 metres. Below that the bands sit closer than the line can separate, and the ages have to come from the flow model.

title: Which marker survives the depth
task: Choose the signal that can still be counted at this depth.
scene: Yuki Tanabe has four yearly signals measured on the same stretch of core, at fourteen hundred metres. A year down there is about twenty-six millimetres thick.
assumes: water can move slowly through the connected air spaces in packed snow
takeaway: A signal is only useful for counting while it is still sharper than the layer it marks.
question: At fourteen hundred metres, which signal can still separate one year from the next?
why: Water keeps moving through the open spaces in packed snow for decades after it lands. That movement smooths the isotope record, and it smooths away anything thinner than the distance it travels. By fourteen hundred metres a year is far thinner than that. Salt and dust do not move. They are grains and specks sitting where they fell, so their yearly pattern survives as deep as anybody can measure it.
answerText: Salt and dust. They sit where they landed, so the moving water never smoothed their yearly pattern away.

choices: Salt and dust, which never moved through the snow.
The isotope ratio, which swings hardest of all at the surface.
The visible banding, which needs no measurement at all.
Electricity, which answers to every acid in the ice.
rebuttals: The isotope swing is biggest at the surface, and it is the first thing the moving water smooths away.
Visible banding depends on bubbles, and the bubbles are gone below a certain depth.
Electricity finds acid, and acid arrives when a volcano erupts rather than every year.

title: How old the bottom of the snow is
task: Turn the sealing depth into an age.
scene: Brandt has the temperature string reading down to eighty-eight metres, which is where the spaces between the grains seal here. The surface adds about a third of a metre of snow a year.
assumes: a depth divided by what one year adds gives a number of years
takeaway: A depth becomes an age only through the rate that filled it.
question: How old is the snow at the depth where the spaces seal?
why: Turning a depth into an age is division. How deep it is, divided by how much one year adds. Up here the layers have not been squashed thinner yet, so one division does it. Deeper down the same sum has to be done bit by bit, because each year is thinner than the one above it. Nearly three centuries of snow sit above the sealing depth here, and every one of those years is still open to the air.
answerText: About 275 years. That is nearly three centuries of snow above the depth where the air gets shut in.

estimate.prompt: The spaces seal at eighty-eight metres. The surface adds about 0.32 metres of snow a year, and this snow has not been squashed thinner yet.
estimate.question: How old is the snow at the depth where the spaces seal?
estimate.relationship: Age = depth ÷ what one year adds.
estimate.explanation: The ice figure is the trap. This depth is measured in snow, so the rate has to be in snow as well.
labels: 0.32 m/yr (what one year adds, as snow)

title: What the ratio says in degrees
task: Turn the isotope shift into degrees.
scene: Tanabe has the isotope readings against depth. The stretch covering the last cold spell sits 1.8 units below today's value. The conversion figure is on the board.
assumes: colder air drops its heavier water first, so the snow that falls last is lighter
takeaway: A conversion figure turns a measurement into a claim, and it is measured rather than assumed.
question: How much colder was that cold spell than today?
why: Water carrying heavier atoms turns to snow first. Air that has cooled further has already lost more of them, so the last snow to fall is the lightest. Over a useful range the reading and the temperature move together in a straight line. How steep that line is belongs to this place, not to physics. So it is measured against the mast. Divide the shift by it, and the answer is in degrees.
answerText: About 2.7 degrees colder. The shift is 1.8 units, and one degree here is worth 0.67 of them.

estimate.prompt: The cold spell sits 1.8 units below today's value. Comparing the record against the weather mast gives 0.67 units for every degree.
estimate.question: How much colder was that cold spell than today?
estimate.relationship: Temperature change = the shift ÷ how many units there are in one degree.
estimate.explanation: The other figure on the board belongs to a different kind of measurement. Using it here gives an answer eleven times too small.
labels: 8.0 units for each degree (a different measurement)

title: How firmly the cooling can be stated
task: State the cooling with the doubt around it.
scene: Brandt has the mast record, the years that overlap it, and the scatter around the fitted line. The season summary needs a statement about that cold spell.
assumes: a line fitted through measurements carries a spread as well as a middle
takeaway: Moving the middle and narrowing the spread are different actions, with different evidence behind them.
question: Which work would let the summary say the spell was more than two degrees colder?
why: The answer is a spread, not a number. The line was fitted through eleven years of overlap, and it carries the scatter of those eleven years. Saying the spell was more than two degrees colder is a claim about where the whole spread sits. So it is won by making the spread narrower. More overlap years is the only thing here that adds information. The correction moves the middle and leaves the spread as wide as it was.
answerText: More overlap with the mast. That narrows the spread, which is what the claim needs. Moving the middle makes the estimate different, not surer.

title: The temperature of what, and where
task: Say what the isotopes are a thermometer of.
scene: Aalto is drafting the summary. He has written that the isotopes give the temperature of the last cold spell. Halvorsen wants that narrowed before it goes out.
assumes: snow forms in a cloud and falls to the ground some way below it
takeaway: A stand-in measures one specific thing, and the sentence has to say which.
question: What does the isotope record most directly record?
why: The isotope ratio is set as water vapour turns into snow. So it records what the cloud was like, weighted to the seasons that bring most of the snow. Getting from there to the ground needs the link between cloud and ground. That is what the site's own figure supplies. The sea the water came off leaves a small mark. The ice's own temperature is a different measurement.
answerText: The temperature where this snow formed, in the air above this place. Close to the ground temperature, and not the same thing.

choices: Where the snow formed, over this region, in the season it fell.
The average yearly temperature of half the planet at that time.
The temperature of the ice itself, kept since it was buried.
The temperature of the sea the water came off.
rebuttals: One site records its own region. An average for half the planet is built by adding many sites together.
A thermometer down the hole measures the ice now. That is a check on the isotopes rather than a replacement for them.
Where the water came from does leave a mark, and it is a small correction rather than the signal.

title: How much younger the air is
task: Work out the gap between the air and the ice around it.
scene: The spaces between the grains seal at eighty-eight metres here. Above that, air moves freely up to the surface. Adeyemi has the yearly build-up on the board beside it.
assumes: air moves through the connected spaces in the snow until they close off
takeaway: A bubble is sealed at a depth, and the ice around it arrived at that depth long before.
question: How much younger is the air than the ice around it?
why: Air moves through the open spaces in the snow. It stays in touch with the sky until those spaces close. So the air in a bubble is about as old as the moment it was sealed. The ice around it is as old as the snow. The gap is how long that snow took to get down there. Cold dry places take centuries. Wet coastal ones take decades. Forget it, and a gas record is plotted centuries too early.
answerText: About 460 years. The snow at the sealing depth is that old, and the air shut into it is nearly new.

estimate.prompt: The spaces seal at eighty-eight metres. The snow above averages 0.62 of the weight of solid ice, and the site adds 0.119 metres of ice a year.
estimate.question: How much younger is the air than the ice around it?
estimate.relationship: Age gap = sealing depth × how heavy the snow is ÷ what one year adds, in ice.
estimate.explanation: The snow thickness is the trap. The weight has already been allowed for, and using it twice counts the same correction twice.
labels: 0.62 (how heavy the snow is, against solid ice)
0.119 m/yr (what one year adds, as ice)

title: From snowfall to sealed bubble
task: Build the stages in order, then name the one that fixes the gap.
scene: Lindqvist has the borehole's own record on the wall. Five stages, from a snowflake landing to air being shut away, with a measurement against each.
assumes: something that passes through several stages is limited by one of them
takeaway: In a chain of stages, one of them sets the answer and the rest follow it.
question: Which stage decides how much older the ice is than the air inside it?
why: Every stage moves something, and only one fixes the size of the gap. Air swaps with the sky all the way down through the snow. So its age hardly changes, while the ice around it gets older year by year. The moment the spaces seal is the moment that swapping stops. Whatever the ice's age is at that depth is the gap. Mixing keeps the air young, and it is worth a decade.
answerText: The moment the spaces seal. The gap is the age of the ice at that depth. Above it, open snow. Below it, a bubble.

title: Why the gas record has no sharp edges
task: Say why the gas record is smoother than the ice record.
scene: Okonkwo has both records from the same depths on one plot. The ice record has features a few years wide. The gas record has nothing in it narrower than a few decades.
assumes: a measurement that averages over a stretch cannot show anything shorter than it
takeaway: A record made by averaging cannot show a change faster than the averaging.
question: Why is the gas record smoother than the ice record from the same depths?
why: Air stays in touch with the sky all the way through the open snow, and the spaces do not all close at once. They close across a stretch of depth, so the bubbles sealed in one layer hold a mixture covering every year that stretch represents. That smoothing belongs to the site. Somewhere with heavy snowfall seals in a decade and keeps sharp features. Here it takes several. Cutting smaller samples cannot undo it.
answerText: The air mixed through the whole open snow column before it was sealed. So each bubble holds decades of sky, not one year of it.

choices: Each bubble holds air mixed over the decades the spaces took to close.
Gas samples are bigger, so they average more ice.
Carbon dioxide changes more slowly in the air than temperature does.
Bubbles leak slowly into each other over thousands of years.
rebuttals: Sample size is a choice and could be made smaller. The mixing in the snow is fixed by the site.
Some changes in the air really are fast, and this record could not show those either.
Bubbles are sealed, and they do not swap with each other on any timescale that matters here.

title: The spike at 1,642 metres
task: Name which eruption the layer came from.
scene: One sulphur spike. Two eruptions of about the same age. Glass fragments from the same centimetre. Okonkwo has the chemistry, the layer count and the modelled age.
assumes: volcanic glass carries the chemistry of the volcano that threw it out
takeaway: A layer is identified by what is in it, not by the date that would be convenient.
why: The glass chemistry is the only reading here that does not depend on the timescale. It is also the one that tells the two apart, because glass carries the fingerprint of the magma it came from. The modelled age cannot choose between two eruptions ninety years apart. Its own doubt is wider than that. Sea salt does not arrive with volcanic glass. And the layer count stopped far above this.
answerText: The northern eruption. The glass chemistry is the one reading that owes nothing to the timescale, and it matches.

choices: The northern eruption, named by the glass chemistry.
The southern eruption, since the modelled age fits it a little better.
Neither. The spike is sea salt.
Cannot be settled until the layer count reaches down to it.
choiceMechanisms: Glass chemistry belongs to one volcano, and it does not depend on the timescale at all.
The model puts this depth slightly nearer the southern date.
Sulphur from the sea can make peaks with no volcano involved.
Nothing can be dated without a count that reaches it.
text.headline: A sulphur spike at 1,642 m, with glass fragments, and two eruptions within a century of each other.

title: What a dated ash layer fixes
task: Say what the dated layer fixes, and what it does not.
scene: Adeyemi has the eruption's date, the depth it sits at, and the carbon dioxide measured from the bubbles in the same piece of core.
assumes: volcanic ash falls out of the sky within a year or two of the eruption
takeaway: A dated layer dates the material it is in, and anything else has to be worked out.
question: What does the dated layer fix?
why: Ash falls onto the surface and is buried with the snow, so it dates the ice it sits in. The air in the bubbles beside it was sealed centuries later, further down. It is that much younger. So a dated layer fixes one of the two clocks in the core, and leaves the other to be worked out. That is why the age gap has to be found before a gas record and an ice record can be compared.
answerText: The age of the ice at that depth. The age of the air in the same piece still has to be reached by taking the gap off it.

choices: The age of the ice at that depth, and nothing else on its own.
The age of both the ice and the air there, since they sit in the same piece.
The age of the air, because the ash and the air arrived together.
How fast snow was falling then, from the thickness of the ash.
rebuttals: The two clocks sit in the same piece of core, and they are not the same clock. That gap is what the offset measures.
Ash lands on the surface. The air at that depth stopped moving centuries after the ash was buried.
A layer thickness gives a snowfall rate only once you already know its age.

title: One clear day, three jobs
task: Decide which job takes the clear day.
scene: Brandt has a forecast with one clear day in it and then four of blowing snow. Three jobs are outstanding, and each takes most of a day.
assumes: a measurement that cannot be repeated should be taken while it can be
takeaway: Order the work by what becomes impossible, not by what feels most important.
question: Which job takes the clear day?
why: Two of these can be done in bad weather and one cannot. The pit is beside the hut and the mast is a short walk along a fixed line. Both survive four days of blowing snow. The stake array runs two kilometres out and has to be seen to be read. Worse, blowing snow moves the very surface the stakes are measuring, so a reading taken afterwards measures something else. The broken core can be redrilled any day.
answerText: The stake farm. It is the only one that cannot be done in blowing snow, and a missed reading is a gap nothing can fill later.

choices: Read and re-level the stakes across the whole array.
Dig and photograph the fortnightly snow pit beside the hut.
Service the mast and download the temperature record.
Redrill the shallow core that broke last week.
rebuttals: The pit is a few metres from the hut door and can be dug in any weather.
The mast is on a fixed line, and its record waits until somebody collects it.
A core that broke can be redrilled whenever the drill is free.

title: What both records rest on
task: Open what each part of the comparison rests on, and keep what stands alone.
scene: Five pieces of the comparison are on Aalto's screen, each worked out from something else. Okonkwo wants to know which of them would still stand if the flow model were wrong.
assumes: two results worked out from one assumption fail together if that assumption fails
takeaway: Two numbers that agree because they came through the same step have not checked each other.
question: Which parts of this comparison would survive the flow model being wrong?
why: Both teams counted layers as far as they could. Then they handed the rest to the same flow model. Below the counts, the two age scales are not two estimates that agree. They are one calculation done twice. What survives the model being wrong is the counted part, which is arithmetic on measured layers, and the ash layer, whose date came from a volcano rather than from ice.
answerText: The counted part, and the ash layer. Everything below the counts on both sides was dated with the same model, so those two agreeing proves nothing about it.

title: How much more carbon dioxide
task: State the change against what it started from.
scene: Adeyemi has carbon dioxide at 190 parts per million through the cold spell, and 280 at the top of the core. Halvorsen wants the change stated plainly.
assumes: parts per million counts how many there are out of every million
takeaway: A rise means most when it is stated against what it started from.
question: How much bigger is 280 than 190, as a percentage?
why: Ninety parts per million sounds small on its own. Everything depends on what it started from. Against a hundred and ninety it is a rise of nearly half. That is the number that matters. What the air does with heat depends on how much of this gas is in it, not on how many parts got added. State a change without its starting point, and a big change reads as a small one.
answerText: About 47 per cent — nearly half as much again as the cold spell had.

estimate.prompt: Carbon dioxide is 190 parts per million in the cold spell and 280 at the top of the core, which is 90 more.
estimate.question: How much bigger is 280 than 190, as a percentage?
estimate.relationship: Percentage rise = the difference ÷ what it started at × 100.
estimate.explanation: Divide by the newer number instead and you get 32 per cent, which answers a question nobody asked.
estimate.solution: Ninety ÷ one hundred and ninety, times a hundred, is about 47 per cent.
labels: 0.67 units for each degree (a different measurement)

title: Half a unit, in degrees
task: Put the difference into the units of the claim.
scene: The two records differ by about half a unit through the cold spell. Tanabe has the site's own figure, and a draft that calls that difference a different climate.
assumes: a difference in units becomes a difference in degrees through the site's own figure
takeaway: A difference has to be put into the units of the claim before anybody can judge it.
question: What is half a unit worth, in the terms the draft paragraph uses?
why: This site's figure is 0.67 units for every degree. Half a unit divided by that is about three quarters of a degree. That is the whole point of converting. In units the difference sounds like a rounding error. In degrees it is a quarter of the cooling the season means to report. Whether it is real climate is a separate argument, and nobody can have it in two different units.
answerText: About three quarters of a degree. Smaller than the cooling being reported, and big enough to matter to it.

choices: About three quarters of a degree, which is a quarter of the cooling being reported.
About half a degree, since one unit is roughly one degree.
Nothing, until the difference is bigger than the scatter on one measurement.
About four degrees, since the figure is in units for each degree.
rebuttals: One unit per degree is not this site's figure, and using it changes the answer by half.
The scatter on one measurement is far smaller than this, which is why anybody noticed it.
Multiplying by the figure instead of dividing by it gives an answer about five times too big.

title: What the correction leaves behind
task: Predict what the correction will leave, apply it, then check against the ash.
scene: Adeyemi has the age gap for both sites, and the means to re-plot both gas records on their own clocks. The ash layer is dated by neither calculation.
assumes: a correction has to be predicted before it is applied, or it cannot be wrong
takeaway: A prediction made before the correction is the only thing that can test it.
question: What is left of the difference once both gas records are on their own clocks?
why: Air keeps mixing with the sky until the snow seals, so the gas is younger than the ice around it. How much younger depends on the sealing depth and how fast snow arrives. Skarv gets four times the snow, so its gap is a fraction of this station's. Plot both on ice clocks and one curve shifts much further. That looks like climate and it is arithmetic.
answerText: About 0.15 of a unit. Most of the difference was the age gap, and what is left sits inside both teams' own doubt.

title: The clock that does not need layers
task: Date ice the counting cannot reach.
scene: Okonkwo has a sample from the deep section. A quarter of the radioactive atoms are left, and the half-life is written on the bench.
assumes: a radioactive atom halves in amount every half-life, whatever else happens to it
takeaway: Where counting has run out, a clock that runs on its own is the only date left.
question: How old is the sample?
why: A radioactive atom decays at a rate nothing in the ice can change. Not temperature. Not pressure. Not flow. Every half-life, half of what is left goes. So a quarter left means two halvings have gone by, which is two half-lives of time. That is a date owing nothing to the flow model, which is what makes it worth having down here.
answerText: About eleven and a half thousand years. Two halvings, at 5,730 years each.

estimate.prompt: A quarter of the atoms are left, which is two halvings. One half-life is 5,730 years.
estimate.question: How old is the sample?
estimate.relationship: Age = the half-life × how many halvings have gone by.
estimate.explanation: One halving leaves a half. Two leave a quarter. Count one instead of two and the answer comes out half as old.
labels: 3,010 m (how thick the ice is here)

title: What is left to disagree about
task: Say what the corrected comparison supports.
scene: Both records are re-plotted, the ash layer lines up in both, and 0.15 of a unit of difference is left. Both teams quote doubt bigger than that.
assumes: a difference smaller than the doubt on either measurement is not a measured difference
takeaway: Explaining a disagreement away is a result, and it is the result that gets published.
question: What does the corrected comparison support?
why: What is left after the correction is smaller than either team's own doubt. So there is no measured difference left to explain. That is a result, rather than the absence of one. Two cores, drilled by different people and put on clocks that match, record the same cooling. The correction does not weaken that. It was predicted first, and then tested against a date neither team produced.
answerText: That the two records agree, and that most of the apparent difference was the age gap rather than climate.

choices: The two records agree, once both are on gas clocks.
The two records disagree, by less than was first thought.
Nothing at all, since a correction had to be applied to get there.
The Skarv record is wrong, since its gap was the smaller one.
rebuttals: A difference smaller than both teams' doubt is not a disagreement of any size.
A correction that was predicted and then tested is evidence, not a weakness.
Both records were on ice clocks. The gap is smaller at Skarv because it snows more there.

title: Six signatures and two hours
task: Spend the two hours on the claims worth checking.
scene: Six lines on the night sheet, all signed. Tanabe has two hours before the flight list closes, and can properly check two of them.
assumes: a signature records that somebody believed something when they signed
takeaway: A signed record is evidence that a claim was made, not evidence that it was true.
question: Which two claims should the two hours check?
why: A signature says somebody believed something at the time. The store reading of minus nineteen says that belief was wrong for part of the night. Two of these claims matter and are carried by nothing but a signature. The store, and the gas samples. Both decide whether measurements on that ice can be defended. The mast keeps its own record. The food and the fuel are the camp's problem.
answerText: The store temperature and the gas samples. Both matter, both are signed with nothing behind them, and both would sink measurements if they are wrong.

title: What comes back first
task: Put the restart in order.
scene: Power is back on one generator. Lindqvist, de Vries and Tanabe each want their own system first. One generator will not carry them all.
assumes: something already being lost is different from something merely waiting
takeaway: Restart in the order of what is still being lost, not in the order of who asked.
question: What gets restarted first?
why: Three of these are waiting and one is going bad. Ice above minus twenty starts losing gas out of the bubbles near its cut faces. That loss cannot be undone or measured around, so every hour is more core that can never answer a gas question. A lost drilling day is a day. The queued samples are as good tomorrow as today. A report sent six hours late is a report sent.
answerText: The core store. It is the only one still losing something for good. Every hour above minus twenty costs measurements nobody can make again.

choices: The core store, which is still warming.
The drill, so the day's run is not lost.
The chemistry line, so the queued samples can be run.
The satellite link, so the season report can go.
rebuttals: A drilling day can be made up, and the drill loses nothing standing idle.
The queued samples are in the store. If the store is warm, they are what is being lost, not the queue.
A report does not go off, and the link is the one thing here that changes nothing by waiting.

title: One year proves nothing
task: Turn thirty years of readings into one number for the period.
scene: Aalto has thirty years of yearly temperatures from the top of the core. The summary wants one number, and one year can swing more than a degree either way.
assumes: averaging many years lets the random part of each one cancel out
takeaway: One year is weather. An average of many years is closer to a climate.
question: What is the average temperature across the thirty years?
why: Every year comes out a little warmer or colder than the run of them, because weather is noisy. Add thirty years and divide by thirty, and those swings cancel out. What is left is much closer to the climate of the period than any one year is. It is also why nobody should read a single warm year as a change. One year here swings more than the difference being argued about.
answerText: Minus 1.8 degrees. That is the climate of the period, and any one year in it can sit more than a degree either side.

estimate.prompt: The thirty yearly values add up to minus fifty-four degrees, and there are thirty of them.
estimate.question: What is the average temperature across the thirty years?
estimate.explanation: One year is not the answer. A single year swings more than a degree either side, which is why the summary quotes thirty of them.
estimate.solution: Minus fifty-four divided by thirty is minus 1.8 degrees.

title: The sentence the record will carry
task: Choose the sentence the evidence reaches.
scene: Four versions of the season's headline claim are on Aalto's screen. All of them are true in some sense. One of them is what the evidence actually reaches.
assumes: a claim is supported when the evidence would have come out differently if it were false
takeaway: An honest claim says what was measured, over what period, and with how much doubt.
question: Which sentence does this season's evidence reach?
why: The first sentence says what was measured, over what stretch, and which part rests on something nobody measured here. The second calls the two records independent. The shared flow model makes that untrue below the counts. The third rounds until the doubt vanishes into the number. The fourth is a claim about every other record at this latitude, and nobody here has read them.
answerText: The one that names the cooling, the period, the doubt, and the fact that the deep dating rests on a model.

choices: A cooling of about 2.7 degrees, with the deep part modelled rather than counted.
A cooling of 2.7 degrees, settled by two independent records.
A cooling of about three degrees, matching the Skarv site.
The biggest cooling ever recorded at this latitude, pending the deep section.
rebuttals: The two records share a flow model below their counts, so independent is the word that fails.
Rounding to three degrees hides the doubt that decides whether this differs from anywhere else.
A superlative is a claim about everybody else's records, and nobody here has read them.

title: What rests on what
task: Match each headline number to what it actually rests on.
scene: Brandt has the season's four headline numbers written up on the hut wall, and an empty column beside each one that nobody has filled in yet.
assumes: a number is only as strong as the weakest step between the ice and it
takeaway: Every number in a record of the past belongs to a class, and the class is part of the number.
why: The four numbers are not the same kind of thing, and the report has to say so. The snowfall is a direct measurement of the surface, and next year's stakes can check it. The cooling is a measurement passed through a conversion, so it carries that conversion's doubt. The age is counted where counting worked and modelled where it did not. The gas amount is well measured, and it hangs on a depth whose age is modelled.

scenarios: Snowfall of 0.119 metres of ice a year
A cooling of 2.7 degrees in the cold spell
An age of 18,400 years at 2,100 metres
Carbon dioxide of 190 parts per million in the cold spell
choices: Measured at the surface, and checkable against next season's stakes.
Measured, then converted through a line fitted to eleven years.
Counted as far as the layers allowed, and modelled below that.
Measured on well-mixed air, at a depth whose own age is modelled.
rebuttals: The cooling is not a direct surface measurement. It arrives through a fitted line.
The age below the counted part cannot be checked against next season's stakes.
The gas amount is well measured, and its date is the modelled part of it.

title: The shortest thing this ice can show
task: Work out how many years get blurred together.
scene: Tanabe has how far water moves through the snow before it seals, and the thickness of a year at the surface. The next team wants to know whether one warm summer could ever be found here.
assumes: water moving through the snow blurs nearby layers into each other
takeaway: A record has a shortest event it can show, and the site sets it rather than the instrument.
question: How many years get blurred together here?
why: Water keeps moving between the grains until the snow seals, and it carries the isotope signal along with it. So anything thinner than the distance it travels gets averaged into its neighbours. Here that distance is about sixteen centimetres of ice, and a year is twelve. So the shortest thing this record can show is a bit over a year. One hot summer sits right at the edge. Deeper down, where a year is millimetres, it has no chance at all.
answerText: A bit over one year. A single hot summer is right at the limit near the surface, and impossible deep down.

estimate.prompt: Moving water blurs about sixteen centimetres of ice together. One year at the surface is about twelve centimetres of ice.
estimate.question: How many years get blurred together here?
estimate.relationship: Years blurred together = how much gets blurred ÷ the thickness of one year.
estimate.explanation: Use the deep layer thickness instead and you answer a different question — what the record can show two kilometres down, which is nearly seven years.
labels: 11.9 cm (one year of ice at the surface)
